newsitem.title: UK: European LPG strong as Mideast, Asia fall again.
newsitem.headline: European LPG strong as Mideast, Asia fall again.

text.p: Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) prices were stronger in Europe as firm crude and naphtha boosted levels this week.
But East Asian demand remained slack and prices fell further there, as Japanese stocks were seen as healthy and there has been no rush to buy in advance of next winter.
Prices for European naphtha, an alternative petrochemical feedstock to propane and butane, climbed over the week and pulled up LPG with it.
"Everything's moved up with naphtha and crude, mainly for large cargoes," said a Scandinavian trader.
A propane parcel was heard done in the low $190's a tonne cif north Germany. But this was an inter-affiliate trade and was reported done on a part fixed price, part formula basis.
Sellers still asked above $190 a tonne cif NWE, the trader said, with propane remaining generally tight. Propane tightened at the end of last month when material was bought for storage.

A seller said he was doing a time swap with another company, moving a 20,000 tonne cargo to Chile at the end of July to take back the same volume in August or September. This exchange was also seen as likely to keep the market tight in the coming weeks.
Small seagoing propane coasters rose sharply over the week.

"There's still demand for contract tonnes, naphtha's up, petchem users are buying, and there's still demand for Morocco and Brazil, all of which have tightened up supply to the point where prices have risen," a coaster trader said.
But he added that current coaster prices, in the high $180's or low $190's a tonne for propane, were not sustainable.
"The buying that needed doing in the short term has been done," and prices are expected to start coming down next week, he said.
The Mediterranean market has been quiet for propane but butane is strong, dealers said, with limited offers.

Spanish energy group Repsol announced at the end of the week that it would invest 12 billion pesetas to build an underground storage unit for LPG near the southern city of Cartagena, with a capacity of 120,000 cubic metres of butane and 80,000 cubic metres of propane.
This will mean the port will become the entry point for around 800,000 tonnes a year of LPG, or more than half of Spain's total demand.
Asian LPG was weak, by contrast to Europe.
"Prices are definitely softening in the east, and fob discounts are coming off in a big way," a trader said.

The discount to the Saudi Contract Price (CP), the benchmark against which most Asian LPG is traded, has widened over the week. Potential buyers are approaching CP - $20 a tonne fob Middle East Gulf, a trader said, while even sellers are down nearly as low as CP - $15 a tonne.

Traders said the differential between the rising North Sea market and falling Middle East prices was widening to the point where movement of Middle East material to Europe was becoming a real possibility, especially given the lack of buying interest in the Asian market.
Japanese buying was seen as minimal.
"Japanese buyers have an interest in waiting as long as they can, and sellers don't want to show their hands," said a trader.

The Japanese level is effectively assessed by adding freight to the Middle East Gulf discounts in the absence of fixed price trade. The last rate heard was $27 a tonne, although it was widely felt that this may fall still further.

South Korea's Korea Petroleum Development Corp announced on Thursday that propane stocks stood at 1.338 million barrels in May, up from 1.099 million barrels in May last year. And butane stocks jumped to 1.362 million barrels in May, up from 665,000 barrels in May 1996.
--Sebastian Alison, London Newsroom, +44 171 542 6412
